title: Heap growth telemetry sleuthing and temporary mitigation notes
body:
Summary:
Observed unexplained heap growth on a subset of serving hosts over a 36-hour window. Symptoms: token-generation latencies climbed, hosts hit OOM-killer on a few low-traffic pods, and continuous-batching queues showed large resident set increases without corresponding connection spikes. This doc captures the on-call sleuthing steps, temporary mitigations applied, commands and telemetry queries used, hypotheses, and follow-ups.

High-level timeline (UTC):
- Nov 01 03:20: first anomaly signal: per-host memory contention alert from cluster-allocator (95th p95 host mem > 85%).
- Nov 01 03:32: SRE pager triggered after automatic scale-up did not relieve memory pressure on three hosts.
- Nov 01 03:40: oncall captured heap profiles from running processes (commands below).
- Nov 02 08:15: selective node restarts reduced memory usage temporarily — but regrowth observed within 6-12 hours.
- Nov 03 17:00: temporary mitigation (reduce continuous-batch window, increase eviction aggressiveness) rolled to affected ASG; memory stabilized on 80% of hosts.

Initial signals and what we looked at:
- Node-level: dmesg OOM kills, cgroup memory.max breaches, kernel logs showing "Out of memory" and process names.
- Process-level: RSS growth in pmap/top, number of resident pages by process, jemalloc stats from /proc/<pid>/maps and admin endpoints.
- Application-level: batch queue depths, per-request KV-cache hits/misses, lingered batch contexts (batch objects persisted beyond request completion).
- Observability: flamegraphs from perf, heap profs (gperftools/heap profiler and jemalloc stats), and our custom allocator metrics (peak_alloc, retained_bytes).

Commands and quick probes used (copy-paste safe):
- ps aux --sort=-rss | head -n 15
- pmap -x <pid> | head -n 30
- cat /proc/<pid>/status | egrep "VmRSS|VmSize|Threads"
- curl -sS http://localhost:9001/debug/alloc-stats | jq .  # internal allocator endpoint
- sudo perf record -p <pid> -F 99 -g -- sleep 30; sudo perf script | stackcollapse-perf.pl > perf.folded; flamegraph.pl perf.folded > perf.svg
- gcore -o /tmp/core.<pid> <pid>  (only when safe; coordinate with owners)

Splunk/observability queries we relied on:
- host.metrics | where metric_name="memory.used_bytes" and env="prod" | stats p95, max by host
- app.logs | where msg like "%batch-context%" and level="error" | timechart count by host
- allocator.metrics | where name in ("jemalloc.retained", "jemalloc.active") | per_minute(avg(value)) by host

Triage notes and rapid hypotheses:
1) Fragmentation vs leak: jemalloc retained vs active grew but RSS growth was larger than active allocations — initial signal points to fragmentation (retained >> active). However, repeated host restarts cleared RSS and growth resumed, suggesting active objects are still being created (possible slow leak with a fragmentation amplification).
2) Long-lived batch contexts: change in continuous-batching rollout three days prior introduced a new batch context lifecycle. We observed objects tagged "batch_ctx" in heap dumps with long lifetimes.
3) KV cache reference cycles: a small subset of requests were causing cache entries to be pinned by linked metadata structures, preventing eviction.
4) Third-party dependency: a library upgrade (vectorized-tokenizer v2.1.0) was deployed to canary and then to partial fleet; it contains a thread-local cache that may hold large buffers and not release promptly under high concurrency.

Immediate mitigation actions taken (ordered):
- Narrow rollout: reverted recent vectorized-tokenizer to v2.0.8 on the affected ASG (hotfix). Result: one host showed 20% lower retained bytes within 30 minutes.
- Reduce continuous-batch max-window from 1.2s to 0.6s for the impacted deployment to avoid long-lived batches accumulating state.
- Apply temporary cgroup memory.max throttle for pods showing growth to force earlier EVICTION not OOM; also bumped K8s pod eviction threshold to prefer pod restart over host OOM.
- Triggered staggered rolling restart of nodes with largest RSS (avoid mass restart).

Results of mitigations:
- Revert of tokenizer produced immediate improvement on canary; production impact correlated in 2–3 hours.
- Shrinking batch window reduced batch_ctx lifetime and host retained bytes trend flattened.
- Cgroup throttle prevented kernel OOM but surfaced application errors (OOM-style failures inside container) in some pods; we added circuit-breaker on those routes.

Deeper debugging artifacts captured:
- Two heapdumps from a leaking process (pid 32411 and 33109) stored in /mnt/diagnostics/heapdumps/ with timestamps.
- jemalloc stats snapshots at t0,t+15m,t+60m attached (jemalloc-retained increased ~3x on affected hosts).
- Perf flamegraphs showing heavy time in tokenizer buffer allocation path (alloc_big_helper).

Root cause hypothesis (current best guess):
A combination of: (A) new tokenizer introduced a thread-local buffer caching behavior that retained large buffers during high concurrency; (B) continuous-batching change allowed per-batch metadata objects to live longer than intended which referenced tokenizer buffers; (C) jemalloc fragmentation amplified retained RSS. Together these paths caused persistent per-request allocations that were not being released promptly, leading to host memory growth.

Open questions / unknowns:
- Exact code path holding final reference to large buffers (need to pin in heapdump).
- Why some hosts were more affected than others (differences in traffic mix, host CPU scheduling, or kernel memory compaction behavior).
- Whether jemalloc purge configuration could have reduced retained growth but at what latency/cost tradeoff.

Immediate follow-ups and assigned owners: (short actionable list)
- Heapdump analysis: Maya to identify top ref-chains for the largest retained objects (due Nov 10).
- Tokenizer revert verification: Ethan to coordinate with releases to confirm no residual canaries remain (due Nov 05).
- Batching lifecycle audit: Priya to instrument batch context creation/expiry counters and expose per-request tag in traces (due Nov 14).
- Allocator tuning experiment: Zoe to run controlled experiment with mallctl purge and aggressive decay settings on a small fleet (due Nov 18).
- Postmortem: draft to include timeline, RCA, mitigations, and long-term tracking (owner: Priya, due Nov 22).

Longer-term mitigations and design changes proposed:
- Add a hard cap on per-batch retained state size and enforce via runtime checks.
- Improve allocator visibility: export jemalloc retained/active per-request via trace headers for top routes.
- Rework tokenizer buffer cache to use weak refs/time-based eviction instead of thread-local persistent caches.
- Add daily low-traffic stress job to trigger full memory compaction on a canary pool to surface fragmentation early.
- Add regression test in CI: under synthetic high-concurrency with batching enabled verify RSS does not grow beyond X% over Y minutes.

Notes about runbook updates needed:
- Add a checklist for memory-growth incidents with exact commands and where to upload heapdumps.
- Document the temporary cgroup throttle steps and safe thresholds.
- Add guidance for when to revert third-party libs vs. instrumenting more.

Appendix: quick checklist for future responders:
1) Capture pid and run: curl -sS http://localhost:9001/debug/alloc-stats > /tmp/alloc-stats.json
2) Dump jemalloc: echo 'prof.dump' > /proc/<pid>/ctl (or use admin endpoint)
3) Take two heapdumps spaced 10–15 minutes apart; upload to /mnt/diagnostics/heapdumps and add link to ticket.
4) Check for recent rollouts (git tags, GH PRs, change control) in the last 72 hours.
5) If suspect library issue, revert on one canary ASG and watch retained bytes for 1–3 hours before wider rollback.

If anything urgent, ping #sre-runtime and escalate to oncall-sre-manager.

-- end of notes --
